Totally recommend this game but there are some things that bother me about it.

Pacing - with all the things I can do, I feel really hurried the whole time, maybe that's intentional but it's just a bit too much for my tastes, a little increase in how long a day lasts would help with that I think.
Then there's the story, once you get the book it just kind of stops until you get the next licenses, but it feels like you should be talking to certain people and find out more about what your dad was up to. Instead you hit a wall and just have to earn more money to continue.

Activities - again maybe its just the game type but a couple of the activities are just a bit too passive. 
The shell cracking for example. You just click essentially, hammer placement doesn't seem to do anything. It's the same mechanic as the simple repairs but there at least your hammer wanders and you have to adjust hit strength. Currently it just feels like a waste of time, you do it after dark to get the pearls but there is really nothing to it.

The bazaar is also a bit boring. You really don't have to think about anything. It even tells you how much change they get. Maybe if you could haggle or they'd try to give you less money for stuff sometimes that would help.

Just a couple thoughts, overall I had fun.

I'm reviewing this just as it released into Early Access and it seems very promising so far. The core loop of cleaning and repairing the ships feels really good. It's simple at first but things get added as you buy more licenses and upgrades -- you can fish, you can crack oysters for pearls, you have a little sales stall, you unlock more difficult repairs that require you to get materials from the store. It's not a deep repair simulator by any means but it has a nice balance of there always being a lot to do without it becoming overwhelming.

I also like the Lovecraft aeshestic, although right now the effects seem kind of limited and madness is pretty easily countered just by puffing the pipe. Still, I don't mind that -- this is a bit more of a relaxing game in general and I like that keeping the madness in check is one more thing to do while still being a manageable task. 

Fun game so far and I really hope it continues development since there is a lot of potential here.

Played the demo and adored it, so when early access came out, I bought it right away! I have a lot of high hopes for this game, and I hope I can offer some input.
-For some reason, the gameplay feels clunkier than the demo did. I'm not sure, something about the flow of going back and forth for materials-- the backpack tool is great, but I suppose it's a bit jarring from the demo's mechanics. Probably just personal preference on my end.
-Working on a boat at night can be annoying, because I cannot see for the life of me what I'm doing, and have to blindly click around to find what I'm supposed to clean up/interact with (the circuit breaker to turn off the lights, specifically). The dark is obviously a huge part of the game, so probably not a light, maybe just a more concise version of the sonar mechanic? 
-I love me a sanity mechanic, but... for lack of a better word, I think the sanity drop is too obvious. Something happens, I see a bunch of red eyes on my screen, I immediately pull up my pipe and it's over with. Maybe making the change less flashy will help; making the sanity increases and decreases apply over time, locking the pipe upgrades behind progress-- I mean, the first thing I did was max out my pipe's upgrades. Maybe you can buy a limited supply of 'higher quality' tobacco at the store that makes it more effective (Put it on a long restock timer, something about it needing to be imported in from elsewhere or something). 
-Another thing to give the sanity mechanic a boost is giving insanity benefits. Maybe you can catch weirder fish when your sanity is low (I haven't done much fishing insane, so this could be in the game already and it flew over my head). Or you can give low sanity consequences! Weird shadows sneaking around and leaving smudge marks you need to clean up. I dunno, I'm kinda just musing here.
OTHERWISE, I HAVE ***ZERO*** COMPLAINTS!!!!!!!!!!!! Eldritch horror cleaning is right up my alley. I'm glad that this game has so much love being put into it.

Overall thoughts: An excellent little management sim. You clean ships, sell goods, and upgrade your space with additional tools and challenges over the course of time. You can customize how your pier looks, give yourself some boosts to assist in accomplishing your tasks, and have some systems automated.

Additionally, you are playing as the son of the original owner of the pier, and trying to discover what happened to him and the eldritch horrors he left behind.

I've only begun to scratch the surface of the deeper story, but the gameplay loop kept me super engaged for a very long while. I kept having the feeling like "just one more day"! To me, that speaks volumes as to how the days engage you.

I'd highly recommend giving this one a try. For less than $10, it's well worth the asking price. :)

Sunken Engine drags you into a chilling, salt-stung world where you’ve inherited your father’s decaying shipyard—and each vessel arriving for repairs holds a secret you’re not supposed to know. As you patch hulls, refit engines, and clean cabins, the boundary between workshop and nightmare starts to blur. The Lovecraftian tone creeps in slowly: odd creaks in the dark, whispers about the sea’s wrath, and strange discoveries hidden under rust and grime.

It’s not a non-stop horror fest, but a game of tension in slow drops—quiet dread, the crackle of old metal, and moments where you realize doing your job might cost your sanity. If you like your horror served with a side of craftsmanship and morose sea stories, this ship is worth boarding.

(Early Access, so expect the weirdest bits to get even weirder.)

While searching for lovecraftian games on steam, this game showed up. It had 0 reviews at the time, but looked intreguing, and I thought I just give it a try. 
And I really enjoyed what I got. For an early access game, it appears to be in a pretty polished state. The graphics are simple, but with an destinct art style, which is quite solid. There are some few textures and elements that stand out, but overall I like the artistic direction quite a bit. Also notable, in the 4,5 hours I played so far, I didn't encounter any bugs or crashes.
The atmosphere and setting is spot on lovecraftian, but doesn't take itself too serious either. There are some "scary" elements, but they didn't really scare me. If this game wants to be a horror game, maybe add a real entity that can appear, attack you and chase you? If not, also fine, the atmosphere is good enough, it doesn't have to be a horror game.
I had fun playing the game, the gameplay loop is engaging and the mechanics are fun. Some aspects could be a litte more polished, like lockpicking (very easy so far, didn't break a single lockpick yet). But for an early access game, it makes a very strong impression.
One thing I would very apprechiate this game to go for is more immersion. There already is a solid basis for it (smoking my pipe in the morning while staring out on the water, after having a nightmare, going to the pub after work to enjoy some beers and play dice, ...), but what I could imagine is to turn the island into a full open world, allowing you to walk through town to the shops, instead of teleporting into them. This would also open up other possibilities, like including some creature that stalkes you from the trees and bushes, or have NPCs walking around, offering dialogue to enhance the worldbuilding, ...
But thats just my two cents on it. Overall, I really enjoy this game so far, and will definitly come back to it. I'm curious on how the devs will enhance it in the future. Keep it up, you're doing a great job so far! :)

Genuinely enjoying this one so far, it's a great example of an EA done right.

The lore is definitely crafted with good attention paid to Lovecraft's work, and is consistent with the many many games we've seen in this type of universe.

The gameplay may be a bit repetitive the first hour or so, but once more upgrades and permits are unlocked you'll find yourself jumping between tasks and rushing to serve all the NPC, while taking a good, long puff from your pipe (which controls the sanity mechanic.
Overall, a great balance of light suspense and satisfying cleaning content, and I love the overall lack of jumpscares (yes, I'm a coward).

Now, that's not to say it's perfect. There are quite a few glitches, the most common of which (at the moment of writing this) is that you don't always get credit for scraping barnacle patches. This leads to incomplete ship cleanups, however the penalty is SO small that it's easy to ignore the issue and wait for a fix.

I've just gotten to some juicier plot parts, and I'm really looking forward to seeing the next bit.

All in all, great little game, runs smoothly, and ABSOLUTELY worth its current price.

First off, I want to say that I really do like this game. I think that they are still in the very beginning faze of releasing a early access so at the time of writing this review, there is still content locks that are showing the footwork of which direction this game is going to grow into and glitches/bugs that are needing to get hammered and smoothed out. Issues that I point out may be fixed and the world may be expanded in following weeks to months to come. There is a reason it is Early Access after all! With that being said... 
[u] Here's the the good, the bad and the ugly.... [/u]

[h3] The Good [/h3]
1. If you love Lovecraftian lore, this is filled with it. The amount of time and dedication that was placed into writing the narrative is detailed. Like any good Lovecraft game, sanity is for sure a important factor for your character and maintaining it is going to be essential for keeping the crazy visions at bay. 

2. If you are a cleaning simulator collector, this is also a great game to play! There are many different tools in your kit on how to complete ship contracts....ranging from tasks such as scrubbing, scraping, hammering, welding and more! Their is much growth in what you can do in the higher tiers and more licenses you attain.
3. While doing these jobs are important to the game, there is other content added in regards to fishing, selling items collected and decorating your place! 
4. The art in the game is simple but creative and speaks to the grimey, dark nature of the lovecraft world. 

[h3] The Bad [/h3]
1. To max out tiers, it doesn't take much and topping out felt quick. The story line is also very quick as well and to follow the path of the story and tasks to complete the story arch doesn't feel like an adventure but rather "go here, see this and now here is the next chapter." 
2. While there is some tutorial pop ups, I felt like I had to go to the settings and check the keybindings right when I first started to play. A few times there was points where I had to google or search the discussions section to figure out why I couldn't do a certain action and what I needed to do. 
3. At some point when you top out, it does feel repetitive. locations of certain cleaning spots are located in the same spots on some ships which does take a little out of the exploration of the vessels. 

[h3] The Ugly [/h3]
1. Don't use a controller. There is updates for a controller, there is key bindings for a controller but until the actual store page says "controller compatible", don't use a controller. Some people posted saying it was super janky but for myself....it froze my character entirely and wouldn't shift back to keyboard settings meaning that I had to windows key + exit game. Even slightly touching the controller will shift it to controller use and it locked my game movements and actions. When I first played, I thought the game didn't work entirely and almost refunded. This is your warning. 
2. You will run into bugs. You will need to respawn at the dock to fix a few bugs. This was pretty constant for me but at least has a work around. You will deal with some sound bugs (one of which is very loud) that won't go away until you exit the game and come back into the game. 
3. As a achievement fanatic, it was very easy and quick to complete 99% of it with one that is just hours of monotonous grinding. 

Once again, I truly do like this game and I think it is worth the buy especially if its on sale. There is many signs in the game that massive expansions are in the works and all of my gripes I have that are ugly and many that I think are bad will most likely be fixed in the future. If you have a hard time dealing with those things as the game develops, wishlist and wait. If you are like me and like to see the bones of a game come full form, absolutely get it.

Sunken Engine, developed by Two Nomads Studio and published by PlayWay S.A., is a darkly atmospheric simulation game that intertwines the routine of ship maintenance with the creeping unease of psychological horror. Set in a decaying coastal town, the game places the player in the role of an inheritor taking over a shipyard once owned by their late father. What begins as a seemingly straightforward task of repairing boats soon reveals itself to be something far more sinister. Every vessel that docks at the yard seems to carry secrets, every repair exposes fragments of a hidden truth, and the legacy you have inherited feels increasingly tainted by something otherworldly. It’s a simulation wrapped in mystery, where the mechanics of hard labor and the weight of personal history collide in unsettling ways.

At its foundation, Sunken Engine functions as a workshop simulator. Players spend their days scrubbing decks, replacing damaged parts, welding broken hulls, and restoring ships to seaworthy condition. There is satisfaction in the work: each completed repair brings income and the ability to invest in better tools, expanded facilities, and upgraded workstations. The gameplay loop has a rhythmic charm—clean, fix, upgrade, repeat—but it is never allowed to become too comfortable. As you settle into the flow of labor, strange phenomena begin to intrude. Tools behave oddly, whispers echo through the yard, and objects move when your back is turned. The sea beyond the docks feels watchful, and your father’s presence lingers like an oil slick across the surface of your memory. This constant tension between the ordinary and the unexplainable gives the game a haunting depth that sets it apart from traditional simulation titles.

Visually, the game embraces a gritty realism that perfectly complements its maritime horror aesthetic. The lighting is subdued, the air heavy with mist and the scent of rust, and the soundscape drenched in creaks, drips, and the low groan of metal under strain. Every ship you work on has its own character—some worn and weather-beaten, others sleek but hiding rot beneath their paint. The detail in the environments reinforces the feeling that the yard itself is alive, steeped in salt and sorrow. Even the smallest tasks carry a weight of atmosphere; cleaning grime from an engine part becomes an act of both maintenance and revelation, as if you’re peeling away the surface of something that shouldn’t be exposed. The developers use subtle visual and audio cues to blur the line between mechanical realism and supernatural dread, crafting an experience that feels immersive and suffocating in equal measure.

Narratively, Sunken Engine unfolds in fragments, through letters, memories, and unsettling discoveries made during your repairs. The story of the protagonist’s father looms large, a man whose obsession with his work seems to have consumed him and possibly invited something unnatural into his world. As you progress, the mystery deepens, and the shipyard’s history begins to intertwine with local legends and strange maritime occurrences. Themes of inheritance, obsession, and sanity underpin the experience, turning every repair job into a step deeper into the protagonist’s unraveling mind. The sanity mechanic reinforces this descent, as exposure to the inexplicable begins to wear down both the character’s composure and the player’s sense of security. It’s not a horror game filled with jump scares or constant danger; rather, its power lies in atmosphere and implication, in the slow erosion of what feels safe.

From a design perspective, the game balances simulation and narrative tension admirably, though not without flaws. As an early access release, it still shows signs of incompleteness—tutorials are minimal, systems occasionally lack polish, and the balance between work and story can feel uneven. Some players may find the repetition of tasks too pronounced, especially in the early stages when progression is slow. Yet these rough edges do little to diminish the game’s potential. The developers’ vision is clear: a tactile, grounded simulation that uses the monotony of labor to heighten the surreal and the horrifying. Each repetitive action draws you deeper into the game’s rhythm, and when the strange intrudes upon that routine, it hits with a quiet but undeniable force.

Sunken Engine stands out as a remarkable fusion of genres—part management sim, part psychological thriller, and part cosmic mystery. Its haunting presentation and deliberate pacing invite patience and reflection, rewarding players who immerse themselves fully in its world of rust, water, and memory. It’s a game about fixing things that perhaps were never meant to be repaired, about confronting decay both physical and emotional. While it may still be evolving in its early state, the foundation it lays is deeply compelling. For players drawn to introspective, atmospheric experiences rather than pure mechanics or adrenaline, Sunken Engine delivers something rare: a sense of unease that lingers long after the last ship has left the dock and the sea has swallowed the sound of your tools.

Original Review 11/22:
I am so sad that I feel I have to write this so others don't fall for this like I did. Genuinely, the gameplay is fantastic. However, the art and seemingly some of the text in this is AI-generated, and as of today 11/12/2025 this is not listed anywhere on the public store page despite it being a requirement on Steam. I thought it looked a little strange at first, but brushed it off thinking I was being overly sensitive. But after some time playing it just became more and more apparent my gut was right. 

There are comments from the devs stating the art "was" AI in the past, and the devs have responded stating that was true but now the characters have been "redesigned". However, its still clearly done through an AI-image program. The prompts that were used have just been updated.

They have the signature AI yellow color wash which is the first sign. There are things that should be straight or somewhat curved that have awkward bends at random points like fishing rods that characters are holding, which is a problem all current AI image generation models struggle with in stylized images. The corners where different items meet are melting into each other such as hair color that seems to flood out of the line art and line art that disappears and reappears randomly. The volumes of characters forms are never consistent.  All characters exhibit the "AI stare" where every single character stares "into the camera" so to speak in the same way with iris's and even eyes that are misshapen from one another. 

For the writing, there is the stereotypical spattering of the emdash (The — line that is longer than a hyphen -) that ChatGPT especially throws into just about every sentence and is something that people would specifically have to use the alt-entry-keycodes to type manually. There is the occasional "Its not just ___, its ____" that ChatGPT throws in everywhere as well.  And in many of the dev-responses to comments and reviews you can see this as well, though for comments I don't honestly care about it being used. I didn't pay for the comments, but I did pay for what I expected to be fully human made content and it was not.

I am certain this will be seen by the devs as they have been very active in their own community, but I implore any and all of the team who sees this to take what I say to heart. I do not feel I am being overly critical. I genuinely enjoy where this game is going and, were it not for the ai-generated content, I would recommend this in a heartbeat. 

But, first, to not have the AI asset usage listed is a violation of Steam's terms of service and I'm not even sure if its allowed period due to the legal can of worms that opens. Second, you have the bones of a fantastic game here, and very clearly care about this project, otherwise you wouldn't have listed it. But you should dedicate that same amount of care to all aspects of it. Yes, its early access and I am not going to pretend that placeholders haven't been a thing for decades, but at the point where you are actually taking money from people, everything, even the placeholders, should be 100% yours. Not 60% yours, 40% midjourney's.

I say this as an artist, I would rather see stick figures or default Unity assets than this. Heck, **I'll** personally draw some filler stuff for it just so that this otherwise great game isn't stained by it. Thats how much I want this to actually succeed. Give me an email to send something to and a bit of time. I understand that the characters have been "re-designed", but if you mean that to say you paid an artist specifically to *draw* these, then they stole from you.
